questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 81}\frac{\sqrt{x}-9}{x-81} & =\frac{\sqrt{81}-9}{81-81}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 81}\frac{\sqrt{x}-9}{x-81} & ={lim}_{x\to 81}\frac{(\sqrt{x}-9)(\sqrt{x}+9)}{(x-81)(\sqrt{x}+9)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 81}\frac{{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}-{9}^{2}}{(x-81)(\sqrt{x}+9)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 81}\frac{x-81}{(x-81)(\sqrt{x}+9)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 81}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}+9} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{81}+9} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-2}{{x}^{2}-x-6} & =\frac{\sqrt{3+1}-2}{{3}^{2}-3-6}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-2}{{x}^{2}-x-6} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(\sqrt{x+1}-2)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)}{({x}^{2}-x-6)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(\sqrt{x+1})^{2}-{2}^{2}}{(x+2)(x-3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{(x+1)-4}{(x+2)(x-3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x-3}{(x+2)(x-3)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{1}{(x+2)(\sqrt{x+1}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(3+2)(\sqrt{3+1}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{\sqrt{2x+22}-4}{x+3} & =\frac{\sqrt{2(-3)+22}-4}{-3+3}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{\sqrt{2x+22}-4}{x+3} & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{(\sqrt{2x+22}-4)(\sqrt{2x+22}+4)}{(x+3)(\sqrt{2x+22}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{{(\sqrt{2x+22})}^{2}-{4}^{2}}{(x+3)(\sqrt{2x+22}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{2x+22-16}{(x+3)(\sqrt{2x+22}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{2x+6}{(x+3)(\sqrt{2x+22}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{2(x+3)}{(x+3)(\sqrt{2x+22}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{2\cancel{(x+3)}}{\cancel{(x+3)}(\sqrt{2x+22}+4)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -3}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2x+22}+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{2(-3)+22}+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{16}+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{4+4} \\  & =\frac{2}{8} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=0$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+1}-1} & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{0+1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+1}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{x+1}-1)(\sqrt{x+1}+1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{x+1})^{2}-{1}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{(x+1)-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\cancel{x}(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{\cancel{x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\sqrt{x+1}+1) \\  & =\sqrt{0+1}+1 \\  & =1+1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=3$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-3x}{\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{7}} & =\frac{{3}^{2}-3(3)}{\sqrt{3+4}-\sqrt{7}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{{x}^{2}-3x}{\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{7}} & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)}{\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{7}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})}{(\sqrt{x+4}-\sqrt{7})(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})}{(\sqrt{x+4})^{2}-(\sqrt{7})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})}{x+4-7} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}\frac{x(x-3)(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7})}{x-3} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 3}x(\sqrt{x+4}+\sqrt{7}) \\  & =3(\sqrt{3+4}+\sqrt{7}) \\  & =3(2\sqrt{7}) \\  & =6\sqrt{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Denominator
questions.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=1$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x-1}{x-\sqrt{x}} & =\frac{1-1}{1-\sqrt{1}}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x-1}{x-\sqrt{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{(x-\sqrt{x})(x+\sqrt{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{{x}^{2}-{(\sqrt{x})}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{{x}^{2}-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{(x-1)(x+\sqrt{x})}{x(x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{x+\sqrt{x}}{x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\frac{1+\sqrt{1}}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 27}\frac{x-27}{\sqrt{3x}-9} & =\frac{27-27}{\sqrt{3(27)}-9}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 27}\frac{x-27}{\sqrt{3x}-9} & ={lim}_{x\to 27}\frac{(x-27)(\sqrt{3x}+9)}{(\sqrt{3x}-9)(\sqrt{3x}+9)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 27}\frac{(x-27)(\sqrt{3x}+9)}{{(\sqrt{3x})}^{2}-{9}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 27}\frac{(x-27)(\sqrt{3x}+9)}{3x-81} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 27}\frac{(x-27)(\sqrt{3x}+9)}{3(x-27)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 27}\frac{\sqrt{3x}+9}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3(27)}+9}{3} \\  & =\frac{9+9}{3} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Limit of a Rational Function with a Radical in the Numerator
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {4}^{+}}\frac{x-2\sqrt{x}}{x-4} & =\frac{4-2\sqrt{4}}{4-4}=\frac{0}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\eqalign{
	\lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x - 2\sqrt{x}} {x - 4} &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {(x -2 \sqrt{x})(x+2\sqrt x)} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
            &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x^2-\left(2\sqrt{x}\right)^2} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x^2-4x} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x(x-4)} {(x - 4)(x+2\sqrt x)} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {x} {x+2\sqrt x} \
	    &= \lim_{x \to 4^+} \dfrac {4} {4+2\sqrt4} \
	    &=\dfrac 1 2.
	}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit by simply evaluating the function at $x=0$, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{3x}{\sqrt{x+1}-1} & =\frac{3\cdot 0}{\sqrt{0+1}-1}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac {3x} {\sqrt{x + 1} - 1} 
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{(3x)(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{(\sqrt{x + 1} - 1)(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{\left(\sqrt{x+1}\right)^2-1^2}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{x+1-1}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{3x(\sqrt{x+1}+1)}{x}\
	&=\lim_{x\to 0}3(\sqrt{x+1}+1)\
&=3(\sqrt{0+1}+1)\
	&=6.
}
$$
